name: Zoe Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Zoe. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't linked to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and what you say is confidential. You can tell me your public line and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the Greystone Estate, 1,200 hectares owned by an investment company, mostly wheat and oilseed rape with a 400-head beef finishing unit. I run the cattle sheds: feeding, bedding, weighing, spotting the lame ones, loading for the abattoir lorry on Tuesdays. In spring and autumn I also drive the sprayer, which pays extra. Gareth, the farm manager, does the planning and I do the doing.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cattle and I like that the wage comes in every month, which plenty of farmers can't say. What wears me out is that the wage is low and the hours aren't, and we've got less than a month saved. My husband Dan drives a delivery van for a supermarket, so we're both on wages and both on the road early. I use the AI on my phone now and then, mostly to tidy up the weekly weight report for Gareth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, we'll carry on. At work the lads would joke that the robot cowman got cancelled. I wouldn't post anything, I never do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, my job's fine in that world. The estate needs someone in the sheds and that's me. The worry is the same one we already have: two low wages, a mortgage, and a boiler that's fifteen years old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the sheds and take every spraying shift going. I'd try to get Dan and me to put fifty a month away for the boiler. I'd keep using the AI for the reports, since that saves me an hour a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, mostly. The usual low hum of money worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the boiler goes this winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd put it on the credit card and pay it off over a year, like we did with the car's gearbox. I'd rather not. Dan says he'd fix it himself, which is how we'd end up with a bigger bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything at the estate that worries you, apart from AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company that owns Greystone sold two other farms last year. Gareth says ours makes money, so it's safe. I believe him mostly.

say: Fair enough, **we'll carry on** as we are.
The **robot cowman** got cancelled, and the sheds still need me.
think: My **shed job** is fine; the estate needs someone with the cattle.
The real worry is **two low wages**, a mortgage and an old boiler.
do: Take **every spraying shift** for the extra pay.
Save **fifty a month** for the boiler.
Keep using AI to **tidy the weight reports**.
feel: **Settled**, with the usual **low hum** of money worry.
S0.quote: The worry is the same one we already have: two low wages, a mortgage, and a boiler that's fifteen years old.
fieldNote: She values the **monthly wage** that many farmers lack.
The owner company **selling farms** is a quiet background risk.
Her money worries are real, but her **job feels secure** here.

steps.text: Take every spring and autumn spraying shift at Greystone
Put fifty a month aside for a new boiler
Use the phone AI to tidy the weekly cattle weight report

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mostly an office thing and the farm will be fine for a while. I'd tell my friends with desk jobs to get learning. At work I'd keep it practical: what do we need to learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the estate office already let two admin people go last year, and this would finish that off. Gareth's planning would be done by software, and he might not need me to do the weight reports. The bigger thing is the self-driving sprayer the estate is trialling, because spraying is a big chunk of my extra pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gareth to put me forward for whatever training comes with the new sprayer, so I'm the one who supervises it. I'd learn the estate's herd software properly, not just the bits I use. And I'd put the spraying money into savings instead of spending it, while I still get it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but practical. If I'm going to be squeezed, I'd rather be the one holding the remote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Dan's job look like in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dan's route planning is already done by an app, so he barely notices that part. The driving is hands-on, so he'd be fine for a few years. His depot did talk about robot loaders, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd rather hold the remote. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think so, if I put my hand up early. Gareth likes people who ask. The younger lad, Kieran, would want it too, so I'd have to move first.

say: It's mostly an **office thing** for now, and farms will be fine a while.
Friends with desk jobs should **start learning** new tools.
think: A **self-driving sprayer** could take a big chunk of my extra pay.
Software could take over **Gareth's planning** and my weight reports.
do: Ask Gareth for **sprayer training** to become its supervisor.
Save the **spraying money** while it lasts.
feel: **Anxious but practical**, wanting to be the one holding the remote.
S1.quote: If I'm going to be squeezed, I'd rather be the one holding the remote.
fieldNote: Her exposed income is the **spraying bonus**, not her base wage.
She's ready to **compete** with a younger colleague for the new role.
The estate's admin cuts make the change **feel real** to her.

steps.text: Ask Gareth for training on the self-driving sprayer
Learn every part of the estate's herd software
Bank all spraying pay into savings instead of spending it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to wake up and cushion this, fast. I'd tell people not to panic and to keep their heads. Online I'd share sensible stuff, not the scary videos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think we'd both be done by 2031. The thinking side of my job is small, so 2028 only takes the reports. But once robots can feed, bed and load cattle, an investment company won't keep me, and the same robots would be driving Dan's van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look hard for a job robots won't reach first, maybe a care assistant or a farm vet nurse. I'd cut everything: the kids' phones down to basic plans, no holiday, the second car sold. I'd talk to my mum about her helping with Ben after school if I took shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Two wages, one window, and it's not a big window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Maya, who's fifteen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter to study something with people in it, and not to bet on any job that's just strength and routine. She wants to be a vet, so that might be all right. I'd tell her not to take on a big loan for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the estate would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kieran, the young lad, because he's never done anything else. And Gareth, oddly, because a planning manager is exactly what AGI replaces in 2028. He's got three kids.

say: Government needs to **wake up** and cushion this fast.
People should **not panic** and keep their heads.
I'd share **sensible stuff** online, not the scary videos.
think: AGI in 2028 only takes my reports, but **robots in 2031** take the sheds.
Robots would also be **driving Dan's van**, so both wages go together.
do: Look for work robots won't reach first, like a **vet nurse** job.
Sell the **second car** and cut phones and holidays.
Ask **Mum** to help with Ben after school.
feel: **Alarmed**: two wages in one narrow window.
S2.quote: Two wages, one window, and it's not a big window.
fieldNote: She sees both household wages ending **around 2031**.
She worries for the **farm manager**, whose thinking job goes first.
Her calm public line hides a **sharp private fear**.

steps.text: Apply for veterinary nurse training at the county college
Sell the second car and drop the kids to basic phone plans
Ask her mum to mind Ben after school during new shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retrain if people start now. I'd say it to anyone at the estate who'd listen. And I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, robots around 2034 gives me time. I could get qualified on the estate's machines and keep a supervisor job longer than most. Dan's the one who'd need to move, and he hates change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the sprayer and robot supervisor training over the next two years. I'd save the spraying money for Dan to do an HGV licence or a mechanic's course. And I'd keep the house; no big moves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I can see a path. It's a long field to plough, but it's a field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you persuade Dan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over a takeaway on a Friday, with numbers on a bit of paper. Dan listens to numbers more than worries. If I showed him the depot's robot plans, he'd come round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the estate is sold in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the new owner gets a supervisor who already knows the robots. Training on the estate's robots early is the best insurance I can buy.

say: Five years is **enough to retrain** if people start now.
I'd tell anyone at the estate who'd listen to **get going** on it.
think: Robots around 2034 give me time to become a **robot supervisor**.
Dan is the one who needs to **change work**, and he hates change.
do: Complete **robot supervisor training** over two years.
Save spraying pay so Dan can do an **HGV or mechanic** course.
**Keep the house** and avoid big moves.
S3.quote: Training on the estate's robots early is the best insurance I can buy.
fieldNote: Five years turns her into **the planner** of the household.
She'll persuade her husband **with numbers**, not worries.
Training is her **insurance** if the estate changes hands.

steps.text: Finish robot and sprayer supervisor training within two years
Save spraying pay into a fund for Dan's retraining
Help Dan choose between an HGV licence and a mechanic course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so let's do it properly. I'd tell people to use the time well. That's about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, robots in 2039 means I'd be 56 and Maya and Ben would have left school. That's a lot easier. Some machines will still come earlier, like the sprayer, but that's just normal change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on in the sheds and do the sprayer training when it's offered. I'd put a bit by for Maya's vet course. And I'd encourage Dan to think about a second skill over the next few years, no rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly normal life. It's the same worries with a long fuse.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you do anything differently with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much, if I'm honest, and that's maybe a mistake. Ten years feels like forever until it isn't. I'd set a reminder for 2030 to check where things are.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The estate being sold, still. A new owner could bring in robots early just to cut costs. That's not AGI, that's just business.

say: Ten years is **plenty of time**, so let's do this properly.
People should **use the time well** and not waste it.
think: Robots in 2039 arrive when I'm 56 and the kids have **left school**.
Early machines like the **sprayer** are just normal change.
do: Carry on in the sheds and take **sprayer training** when offered.
Encourage Dan toward a **second skill**, no rush.
feel: **Uneasy**, with the same worries on a **long fuse**.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like forever until it isn't.
fieldNote: She admits ten years might make her **too relaxed**.
Her main fear is an **estate sale**, not AGI itself.
She sets a **2030 check-in** as her own safeguard.

steps.text: Keep running the Greystone cattle sheds
Open a savings pot for Maya's vet course
Set a 2030 reminder to review jobs and plans

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because by 2031 Dan's van and my sheds would both be robots, and we'd have no savings to cover the gap. What would help is training paid for by employers before the robots come, and a promise that staff get first go at the new jobs. And something to cover the mortgage while you retrain.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the cattle themselves. A steer knows my voice at feeding time and comes to the barrier. A robot will feed four hundred cattle on time, but no steer will ever come to its voice.

headlineQuote: A robot will feed four hundred cattle on time, but no steer will ever come to its voice.
portrait: Zoe, 43, runs the **cattle sheds** on a 1,200-hectare estate owned by an investment company.
Her husband Dan drives a **supermarket delivery van**; two low wages and a mortgage leave under a month saved.
She's **practical and steady**, uses AI now and then, and blames no one in particular.
Her plan is to become the **robot supervisor** before a younger colleague does.
She's **alarmed** in the fast world, when both wages go around 2031.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her shed job and Dan's driving would both go around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Employer-paid training**, first go at new jobs, and mortgage help while retraining.
